Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 109, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ikrimah.

It is Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and to Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Medina."

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Jabir, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this surah and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in the two rak'ahs of the tawaf."

Also in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib some twenty times, or about ten times: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

al-Hakim narrated and graded as sahih from Ubayy, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would perform the witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Muhammad ibn Nasr and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ equals one third of the Qur'an, and ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ equals one quarter of the Qur'an, and he used to recite both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ it is for him equal to a quarter of the Qur'an.'"

al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ it is as if he recited a quarter of the Qur'an, and whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ it is as if he recited a third of the Qur'an."

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, al-Baghawi, and Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his Targhib narrated from a shaykh who met the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and he passed by a man reciting ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and he said: 'As for this one, he has been freed from shirk.' Then another was reciting ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By it, Paradise has become obligatory for him.'" In another narration: "As for this one, he has been forgiven."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from his father, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, teach me what I should say when I go to my bed. He said: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, then sleep upon its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i, from his father, as a marfu' report, the same as it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Ashja'i: 'When you come to your resting place for sleep, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, for when you say it, you have become free from shirk.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from al-Harith ibn Jabalah, and al-Tabarani said from Jabalah ibn Harithah, who is the brother of Zayd ibn Harithah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me something to say when I sleep. He said: 'When you take your resting place at night, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until you reach its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not direct you to a word that will save you from associating partners with Allah: that you recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khabbab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you take your resting place, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) never came to his bed except that he recited ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until he finished."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever meets Allah with two surahs, there is no reckoning for him: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Durays narrated from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in a night, he has done much and done well."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The alif and lam in ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ are for the category (li-l-jins). However, since the verse is addressed to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge would die upon their disbelief (p-1662), the intended meaning of this generality is the specific group of those who were like that; for among the disbelievers at the time of the revelation of this verse were those who embraced Islam and worshipped Allah, glorified be He.

The occasion of revelation of this surah is that the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to worship their gods for a year, and they would worship his God for a year.

So Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to say to them: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning: I will not do what you demand of me, namely worshipping what you worship of idols. It was said that the intended meaning concerns the future time, because the negating particle lā (not) generally does not enter except upon the present-future imperfect verb, just as mā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the present.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor will you do in the future what I demand from you of worshipping my God.

﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: nor have I ever, in what has passed, been a worshipper of what you have worshipped, and the sense is: this has not been known of me.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor have you worshipped at any time what I am upon worshipping. So it was said, and this is according to the opinion of the one who said there is no repetition in these verses, because the first clause is for negating worship in the future, for the reason we previously mentioned that lā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the future. The evidence for this is that lan is an emphasis of what lā negates.

al-Khalil said regarding "lan": its origin is lā, so the meaning is: I will not worship what you worship in the future, nor will you be worshippers in the future of what I seek of worship of my God.

Then he said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: and I am not, at present, a worshipper of your worshipped, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my worshipped.

It was also said the opposite of this, namely that the first two clauses are for the present, and the last two clauses are for the future, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as if someone said: "I am striking Zayd, and I am killing 'Amr," for it is not understood from it except the future.

al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: I will not worship, from now on, what you worship; nor will you be worshippers, from now on, of what I worship; nor am I, in the future, a worshipper of what you have worshipped; nor will you, in the future, be worshippers of what I worship.

al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) negated by this surah his worshipping of their gods for himself, both at present and in the future, and he negated for them the worship of Allah, both at present and in the future.

It was said that each of them is suitable for both the present and the future, but we specify one of them for the present and the second for the future, to avoid repetition.

All of this contains from artificiality and forcing what is not hidden from an impartial person. As for making His saying "nor will I worship what you worship" refer to the future, although it is correct according to the requirement of the Arabic language, it does not work to make His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ refer to the future; because the clause is nominal, and it indicates permanence and constancy at all times, so the entry of negation upon it removes what it indicates of permanence and constancy at all times. And if its being taken as the future were correct, the same would apply to His saying ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ and to His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, so the saying that the two latter clauses refer to the present does not hold. And just as this is refuted, the opposite of what was said is refuted too; because the second, third, and fourth clauses are all nominal clauses introduced by pronouns, which are the subject in each of them, reporting about it with the active participle that governs what follows it, all negated by a single particle, namely the word lā in each of them. So how can it be valid, with this unity, to claim that their meanings in the present and the future are different?

As for the statement of the one who said that each of them is suitable for the present and the future, it is an admission by him of repetition; for taking this in one sense and that in another sense while the wording is one is a matter of arbitrary decision for which no evidence points.

Once this is established for you, know that the Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, and among their practices which cannot be denied and their usages which cannot be rejected is that when they want emphasis they repeat, just as among their practices is that when they want brevity they be concise. This is known to everyone who has knowledge of the Arabic language, and this does not need proof, for proof is sought only for what is obscure, and is demonstrated only for what is disputed.

As for what is so clear, evident, and manifest that no doubter doubts it and no skeptic is uncertain about it, it needs no lengthening and no multiplying of talk and debate.

Among this there occurs in the Qur'an what every reciter of the Qur'an knows, and it perhaps abounds in some surahs, as in Surah al-Rahman and Surah al-Mursalat. In the poetry of the Arabs there is from this what cannot be enumerated, and among it is the saying of the poet:

"O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb; O Bakr, where, where is the flight?"

And another's saying:

"Would that you had asked the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, where, where is ours?"

And another's saying:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, the best of Tamim, all of it, and its most noble."

And another's saying:

"Ah, O you, be safe, then be safe, then be safe, three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And another's saying:

"O Ja'far, O Ja'far, O Ja'far, if I am short, you are shorter."

And another's saying:

"Your pursuers have come to you, your pursuers have come to you; hold back, hold back."

It is established from the Truthful and Truly Believed One (ﷺ), and he was the most eloquent of those who spoke the tongue of the Arabs, that when he spoke a word he would repeat it three times. When you know this, the benefit of the emphasis that occurs in the surah is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would answer them in what they asked of him, namely worshipping their gods. Allah, glorified be He, expressed with "mā," which is used for non-rational beings, in the four positions, because that is permissible, as in His saying: "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" and similar; and the point of this is that the speech proceeds in one pattern and does not vary.

It was said that He intended the attribute, as if He said: I do not worship falsehood, and you do not worship truth.

It was said that "mā" in the four positions is the verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) and not the relative: that is, "I do not worship your worship, and you are not worshippers of my worship," etc.

The clause ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is a resumptive clause establishing His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as His saying ﴿and for me is my religion﴾ establishes His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places (p-1663): that is, if you are content with your religion, then I am content with my religion, as in His saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139]. The meaning is: your religion, which is polytheism, is restricted to being attained by you and does not pass beyond you to being attained by me, as you hope; and my religion, which is monotheism, is restricted to being attained by me and does not pass beyond me to being attained by you.

It was said the meaning is: for you is your recompense, and for me is my recompense; because religion means recompense.

It was said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and it was said it is not abrogated, because they are statements, and statements are not subject to abrogation.

Al-Jumhur read the yā' in His saying "wa-liya" with sukun; Nafi', Hisham, Hafs, and al-Bazzi read it with fatah.

Al-Jumhur also read with the deletion of the yā' in "dini," both in pause and in continuation; Nasr ibn 'Asim, Salam, and Ya'qub retained it both in continuation and in pause.

They said: because it is a noun, it is not deleted.

It is answered that its deletion for the sake of the rhyme-endings (fawasil) is permissible even though it is a noun.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 109, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 2):

وقَدْ أخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، والطَّبَرانِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ «أنَّ قُرَيْشًا دَعَتْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ إلى أنْ يُعْطُوهُ مالًا فَيَكُونُ أغْنى رَجُلٍ بِمَكَّةَ ويُزَوِّجُوهُ ما أرادَ مِنَ النِّساءِ، فَقالُوا: هَذا لَكَ يا مُحَمَّدُ وكُفَّ عَنْ شَتْمِ آلِهَتِنا ولا تَذْكُرْها بِسُوءٍ، فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ فَإنّا نَعْرِضُ عَلَيْكَ خَصْلَةً واحِدَةً ولَكَ فِيها صَلاحٌ، قالَ: ما هي ؟ قالُوا: تَعْبُدُ آلِهَتَنا سَنَةً ونَعْبُدُ إلَهَكَ سَنَةً، قالَ: حَتّى أنْظُرَ ما يَأْتِينِي مِن رَبِّي، فَجاءَ الوَحْيُ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ ﴿لا أعْبُدُ ما تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ، وأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ أفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ تَأْمُرُونِّي أعْبُدُ أيُّها الجاهِلُونَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٤] إلى قَوْلِهِ: ﴿بَلِ اللَّهَ فاعْبُدْ وكُنْ مِنَ الشّاكِرِينَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٦]» .

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to accept wealth from them, so that he would become the richest man in Makkah, and that they would marry him to whichever women he wished. They said: 'This is for you, O Muhammad, but cease reviling our gods and do not speak ill of them. If you do not do so, we offer you one proposal, and in it there is benefit for you.' He said: 'What is it?' They said: 'You worship our gods for one year, and we will worship your God for one year.' He said: 'Wait until I see what comes to me from my Lord.' Then revelation came from Allah: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ to the end of the surah. And Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64] to His words: ﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the thankful﴾ [al-Zumar: 66]."

وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، وابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ في المَصاحِفِ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ مِينا مَوْلى أبِي البُحْتُرِيِّ قالَ لَقِيَ الوَلِيدُ بْنُ المُغِيرَةِ، والعاصُ بْنُ وائِلٍ، والأسْوَدُ بْنُ المُطَّلِبِ، وأُمَيَّةُ بْنُ خَلَفٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قالُوا: يا مُحَمَّدُ هَلُمَّ فَلْنَعْبُدْ ما تَعْبُدُ وتَعْبُدْ ما نَعْبُدُ، ونَشْتَرِكْ نَحْنُ وأنْتَ في أمْرِنا كُلِّهِ، فَإنْ كانَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ كُنْتَ قَدْ أخَذْتَ مِنهُ حَظًّا، وإنْ كانَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ كُنّا قَدْ أخَذْنا مِنهُ حَظًّا، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in (his book) al-Masahif (the codices of the Qur'an) narrated from Sa'id ibn Mina, the mawla (freedman) of Abu al-Bukhturi, who said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship and you worship what we worship, and let us share with you in all of our affair. If what we follow is more correct than what you follow, you will have taken a share of it, and if what you follow is more correct than what we follow, we will have taken a share of it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ to the end of the surah."

وأخْرَجَ عَبْدُ بْنُ حُمَيْدٍ، وابْنُ المُنْذِرِ، وابْنُ مَرْدَوَيْهِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّ قُرَيْشًا قالَتْ: لَوِ اسْتَلَمْتَ آلِهَتَنا لَعَبَدْنا إلَهَكَ، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ السُّورَةَ كُلَّها.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that Quraysh said: "If you touched our gods, we would worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾, the whole surah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever meets Allah with two surahs, there is no reckoning for him: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Durays narrated from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in a night, he has done much and done well."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The alif and lam in ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ are for the category (li-l-jins). However, since the verse is addressed to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge would die upon their disbelief (p-1662), the intended meaning of this generality is the specific group of those who were like that; for among the disbelievers at the time of the revelation of this verse were those who embraced Islam and worshipped Allah, glorified be He.

The occasion of revelation of this surah is that the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to worship their gods for a year, and they would worship his God for a year.

So Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to say to them: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning: I will not do what you demand of me, namely worshipping what you worship of idols. It was said that the intended meaning concerns the future time, because the negating particle lā (not) generally does not enter except upon the present-future imperfect verb, just as mā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the present.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor will you do in the future what I demand from you of worshipping my God.

﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: nor have I ever, in what has passed, been a worshipper of what you have worshipped, and the sense is: this has not been known of me.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor have you worshipped at any time what I am upon worshipping. So it was said, and this is according to the opinion of the one who said there is no repetition in these verses, because the first clause is for negating worship in the future, for the reason we previously mentioned that lā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the future. The evidence for this is that lan is an emphasis of what lā negates.

al-Khalil said regarding "lan": its origin is lā, so the meaning is: I will not worship what you worship in the future, nor will you be worshippers in the future of what I seek of worship of my God.

Then he said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: and I am not, at present, a worshipper of your worshipped, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my worshipped.

It was also said the opposite of this, namely that the first two clauses are for the present, and the last two clauses are for the future, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as if someone said: "I am striking Zayd, and I am killing 'Amr," for it is not understood from it except the future.

al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: I will not worship, from now on, what you worship; nor will you be worshippers, from now on, of what I worship; nor am I, in the future, a worshipper of what you have worshipped; nor will you, in the future, be worshippers of what I worship.

al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) negated by this surah his worshipping of their gods for himself, both at present and in the future, and he negated for them the worship of Allah, both at present and in the future.

It was said that each of them is suitable for both the present and the future, but we specify one of them for the present and the second for the future, to avoid repetition.

All of this contains from artificiality and forcing what is not hidden from an impartial person. As for making His saying "nor will I worship what you worship" refer to the future, although it is correct according to the requirement of the Arabic language, it does not work to make His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ refer to the future; because the clause is nominal, and it indicates permanence and constancy at all times, so the entry of negation upon it removes what it indicates of permanence and constancy at all times. And if its being taken as the future were correct, the same would apply to His saying ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ and to His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, so the saying that the two latter clauses refer to the present does not hold. And just as this is refuted, the opposite of what was said is refuted too; because the second, third, and fourth clauses are all nominal clauses introduced by pronouns, which are the subject in each of them, reporting about it with the active participle that governs what follows it, all negated by a single particle, namely the word lā in each of them. So how can it be valid, with this unity, to claim that their meanings in the present and the future are different?

As for the statement of the one who said that each of them is suitable for the present and the future, it is an admission by him of repetition; for taking this in one sense and that in another sense while the wording is one is a matter of arbitrary decision for which no evidence points.

Once this is established for you, know that the Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, and among their practices which cannot be denied and their usages which cannot be rejected is that when they want emphasis they repeat, just as among their practices is that when they want brevity they be concise. This is known to everyone who has knowledge of the Arabic language, and this does not need proof, for proof is sought only for what is obscure, and is demonstrated only for what is disputed.

As for what is so clear, evident, and manifest that no doubter doubts it and no skeptic is uncertain about it, it needs no lengthening and no multiplying of talk and debate.

Among this there occurs in the Qur'an what every reciter of the Qur'an knows, and it perhaps abounds in some surahs, as in Surah al-Rahman and Surah al-Mursalat. In the poetry of the Arabs there is from this what cannot be enumerated, and among it is the saying of the poet:

"O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb; O Bakr, where, where is the flight?"

And another's saying:

"Would that you had asked the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, where, where is ours?"

And another's saying:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, the best of Tamim, all of it, and its most noble."

And another's saying:

"Ah, O you, be safe, then be safe, then be safe, three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And another's saying:

"O Ja'far, O Ja'far, O Ja'far, if I am short, you are shorter."

And another's saying:

"Your pursuers have come to you, your pursuers have come to you; hold back, hold back."

It is established from the Truthful and Truly Believed One (ﷺ), and he was the most eloquent of those who spoke the tongue of the Arabs, that when he spoke a word he would repeat it three times. When you know this, the benefit of the emphasis that occurs in the surah is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would answer them in what they asked of him, namely worshipping their gods. Allah, glorified be He, expressed with "mā," which is used for non-rational beings, in the four positions, because that is permissible, as in His saying: "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" and similar; and the point of this is that the speech proceeds in one pattern and does not vary.

It was said that He intended the attribute, as if He said: I do not worship falsehood, and you do not worship truth.

It was said that "mā" in the four positions is the verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) and not the relative: that is, "I do not worship your worship, and you are not worshippers of my worship," etc.

The clause ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is a resumptive clause establishing His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as His saying ﴿and for me is my religion﴾ establishes His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places (p-1663): that is, if you are content with your religion, then I am content with my religion, as in His saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139]. The meaning is: your religion, which is polytheism, is restricted to being attained by you and does not pass beyond you to being attained by me, as you hope; and my religion, which is monotheism, is restricted to being attained by me and does not pass beyond me to being attained by you.

It was said the meaning is: for you is your recompense, and for me is my recompense; because religion means recompense.

It was said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and it was said it is not abrogated, because they are statements, and statements are not subject to abrogation.

Al-Jumhur read the yā' in His saying "wa-liya" with sukun; Nafi', Hisham, Hafs, and al-Bazzi read it with fatah.

Al-Jumhur also read with the deletion of the yā' in "dini," both in pause and in continuation; Nasr ibn 'Asim, Salam, and Ya'qub retained it both in continuation and in pause.

They said: because it is a noun, it is not deleted.

It is answered that its deletion for the sake of the rhyme-endings (fawasil) is permissible even though it is a noun.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to accept wealth from them, so that he would become the richest man in Makkah, and that they would marry him to whichever women he wished. He said: 'What is it?' They said: 'You worship our gods for one year, and we will worship your God for one year.' He said: 'Wait until I see what comes to me from my Lord.' Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to accept wealth from them, so that he would become the richest man in Makkah, and that they would marry him to whichever women he wished. They said: 'This is for you, O Muhammad, but cease reviling our gods and do not speak ill of them. If you do not do so, we offer you one proposal, and in it there is benefit for you.' He said: 'What is it?' They said: 'You worship our gods for one year, and we will worship your God for one year.' He said: 'Wait until I see what comes to me from my Lord.' Then revelation came from Allah: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ to the end of the surah. And Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64] to His words: ﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the thankful﴾ [al-Zumar: 66]."

وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، وابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ في المَصاحِفِ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ مِينا مَوْلى أبِي البُحْتُرِيِّ قالَ لَقِيَ الوَلِيدُ بْنُ المُغِيرَةِ، والعاصُ بْنُ وائِلٍ، والأسْوَدُ بْنُ المُطَّلِبِ، وأُمَيَّةُ بْنُ خَلَفٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قالُوا: يا مُحَمَّدُ هَلُمَّ فَلْنَعْبُدْ ما تَعْبُدُ وتَعْبُدْ ما نَعْبُدُ، ونَشْتَرِكْ نَحْنُ وأنْتَ في أمْرِنا كُلِّهِ، فَإنْ كانَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ كُنْتَ قَدْ أخَذْتَ مِنهُ حَظًّا، وإنْ كانَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ كُنّا قَدْ أخَذْنا مِنهُ حَظًّا، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in (his book) al-Masahif (the codices of the Qur'an) narrated from Sa'id ibn Mina, the mawla (freedman) of Abu al-Bukhturi, who said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship and you worship what we worship, and let us share with you in all of our affair. If what we follow is more correct than what you follow, you will have taken a share of it, and if what you follow is more correct than what we follow, we will have taken a share of it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ to the end of the surah."

وأخْرَجَ عَبْدُ بْنُ حُمَيْدٍ، وابْنُ المُنْذِرِ، وابْنُ مَرْدَوَيْهِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّ قُرَيْشًا قالَتْ: لَوِ اسْتَلَمْتَ آلِهَتَنا لَعَبَدْنا إلَهَكَ، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ السُّورَةَ كُلَّها.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that Quraysh said: "If you touched our gods, we would worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾, the whole surah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 109, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ikrimah.

It is Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and to Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Medina."

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Jabir, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this surah and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in the two rak'ahs of the tawaf."

Also in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib some twenty times, or about ten times: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

al-Hakim narrated and graded as sahih from Ubayy, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would perform the witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Muhammad ibn Nasr and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ equals one third of the Qur'an, and ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ equals one quarter of the Qur'an, and he used to recite both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ it is for him equal to a quarter of the Qur'an.'"

al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ it is as if he recited a quarter of the Qur'an, and whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ it is as if he recited a third of the Qur'an."

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, al-Baghawi, and Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his Targhib narrated from a shaykh who met the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and he passed by a man reciting ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and he said: 'As for this one, he has been freed from shirk.' Then another was reciting ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By it, Paradise has become obligatory for him.'" In another narration: "As for this one, he has been forgiven."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from his father, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, teach me what I should say when I go to my bed. He said: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, then sleep upon its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i, from his father, as a marfu' report, the same as it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Ashja'i: 'When you come to your resting place for sleep, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, for when you say it, you have become free from shirk.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from al-Harith ibn Jabalah, and al-Tabarani said from Jabalah ibn Harithah, who is the brother of Zayd ibn Harithah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me something to say when I sleep. He said: 'When you take your resting place at night, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until you reach its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not direct you to a word that will save you from associating partners with Allah: that you recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khabbab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you take your resting place, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) never came to his bed except that he recited ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until he finished."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever meets Allah with two surahs, there is no reckoning for him: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Durays narrated from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in a night, he has done much and done well."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The alif and lam in ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ are for the category (li-l-jins). However, since the verse is addressed to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge would die upon their disbelief (p-1662), the intended meaning of this generality is the specific group of those who were like that; for among the disbelievers at the time of the revelation of this verse were those who embraced Islam and worshipped Allah, glorified be He.

The occasion of revelation of this surah is that the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to worship their gods for a year, and they would worship his God for a year.

So Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to say to them: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning: I will not do what you demand of me, namely worshipping what you worship of idols. It was said that the intended meaning concerns the future time, because the negating particle lā (not) generally does not enter except upon the present-future imperfect verb, just as mā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the present.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor will you do in the future what I demand from you of worshipping my God.

﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: nor have I ever, in what has passed, been a worshipper of what you have worshipped, and the sense is: this has not been known of me.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor have you worshipped at any time what I am upon worshipping. So it was said, and this is according to the opinion of the one who said there is no repetition in these verses, because the first clause is for negating worship in the future, for the reason we previously mentioned that lā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the future. The evidence for this is that lan is an emphasis of what lā negates.

al-Khalil said regarding "lan": its origin is lā, so the meaning is: I will not worship what you worship in the future, nor will you be worshippers in the future of what I seek of worship of my God.

Then he said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: and I am not, at present, a worshipper of your worshipped, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my worshipped.

It was also said the opposite of this, namely that the first two clauses are for the present, and the last two clauses are for the future, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as if someone said: "I am striking Zayd, and I am killing 'Amr," for it is not understood from it except the future.

al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: I will not worship, from now on, what you worship; nor will you be worshippers, from now on, of what I worship; nor am I, in the future, a worshipper of what you have worshipped; nor will you, in the future, be worshippers of what I worship.

al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) negated by this surah his worshipping of their gods for himself, both at present and in the future, and he negated for them the worship of Allah, both at present and in the future.

It was said that each of them is suitable for both the present and the future, but we specify one of them for the present and the second for the future, to avoid repetition.

All of this contains from artificiality and forcing what is not hidden from an impartial person. As for making His saying "nor will I worship what you worship" refer to the future, although it is correct according to the requirement of the Arabic language, it does not work to make His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ refer to the future; because the clause is nominal, and it indicates permanence and constancy at all times, so the entry of negation upon it removes what it indicates of permanence and constancy at all times. And if its being taken as the future were correct, the same would apply to His saying ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ and to His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, so the saying that the two latter clauses refer to the present does not hold. And just as this is refuted, the opposite of what was said is refuted too; because the second, third, and fourth clauses are all nominal clauses introduced by pronouns, which are the subject in each of them, reporting about it with the active participle that governs what follows it, all negated by a single particle, namely the word lā in each of them. So how can it be valid, with this unity, to claim that their meanings in the present and the future are different?

As for the statement of the one who said that each of them is suitable for the present and the future, it is an admission by him of repetition; for taking this in one sense and that in another sense while the wording is one is a matter of arbitrary decision for which no evidence points.

Once this is established for you, know that the Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, and among their practices which cannot be denied and their usages which cannot be rejected is that when they want emphasis they repeat, just as among their practices is that when they want brevity they be concise. This is known to everyone who has knowledge of the Arabic language, and this does not need proof, for proof is sought only for what is obscure, and is demonstrated only for what is disputed.

As for what is so clear, evident, and manifest that no doubter doubts it and no skeptic is uncertain about it, it needs no lengthening and no multiplying of talk and debate.

Among this there occurs in the Qur'an what every reciter of the Qur'an knows, and it perhaps abounds in some surahs, as in Surah al-Rahman and Surah al-Mursalat. In the poetry of the Arabs there is from this what cannot be enumerated, and among it is the saying of the poet:

"O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb; O Bakr, where, where is the flight?"

And another's saying:

"Would that you had asked the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, where, where is ours?"

And another's saying:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, the best of Tamim, all of it, and its most noble."

And another's saying:

"Ah, O you, be safe, then be safe, then be safe, three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And another's saying:

"O Ja'far, O Ja'far, O Ja'far, if I am short, you are shorter."

And another's saying:

"Your pursuers have come to you, your pursuers have come to you; hold back, hold back."

It is established from the Truthful and Truly Believed One (ﷺ), and he was the most eloquent of those who spoke the tongue of the Arabs, that when he spoke a word he would repeat it three times. When you know this, the benefit of the emphasis that occurs in the surah is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would answer them in what they asked of him, namely worshipping their gods. Allah, glorified be He, expressed with "mā," which is used for non-rational beings, in the four positions, because that is permissible, as in His saying: "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" and similar; and the point of this is that the speech proceeds in one pattern and does not vary.

It was said that He intended the attribute, as if He said: I do not worship falsehood, and you do not worship truth.

It was said that "mā" in the four positions is the verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) and not the relative: that is, "I do not worship your worship, and you are not worshippers of my worship," etc.

The clause ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is a resumptive clause establishing His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as His saying ﴿and for me is my religion﴾ establishes His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places (p-1663): that is, if you are content with your religion, then I am content with my religion, as in His saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139]. The meaning is: your religion, which is polytheism, is restricted to being attained by you and does not pass beyond you to being attained by me, as you hope; and my religion, which is monotheism, is restricted to being attained by me and does not pass beyond me to being attained by you.

It was said the meaning is: for you is your recompense, and for me is my recompense; because religion means recompense.

It was said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and it was said it is not abrogated, because they are statements, and statements are not subject to abrogation.

Al-Jumhur read the yā' in His saying "wa-liya" with sukun; Nafi', Hisham, Hafs, and al-Bazzi read it with fatah.

Al-Jumhur also read with the deletion of the yā' in "dini," both in pause and in continuation; Nasr ibn 'Asim, Salam, and Ya'qub retained it both in continuation and in pause.

They said: because it is a noun, it is not deleted.

It is answered that its deletion for the sake of the rhyme-endings (fawasil) is permissible even though it is a noun.

وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، وابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ في المَصاحِفِ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ مِينا مَوْلى أبِي البُحْتُرِيِّ قالَ لَقِيَ الوَلِيدُ بْنُ المُغِيرَةِ، والعاصُ بْنُ وائِلٍ، والأسْوَدُ بْنُ المُطَّلِبِ، وأُمَيَّةُ بْنُ خَلَفٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قالُوا: يا مُحَمَّدُ هَلُمَّ فَلْنَعْبُدْ ما تَعْبُدُ وتَعْبُدْ ما نَعْبُدُ، ونَشْتَرِكْ نَحْنُ وأنْتَ في أمْرِنا كُلِّهِ، فَإنْ كانَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ كُنْتَ قَدْ أخَذْتَ مِنهُ حَظًّا، وإنْ كانَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ كُنّا قَدْ أخَذْنا مِنهُ حَظًّا، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in (his book) al-Masahif (the codices of the Qur'an) narrated from Sa'id ibn Mina, the mawla (freedman) of Abu al-Bukhturi, who said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship and you worship what we worship, and let us share with you in all of our affair. If what we follow is more correct than what you follow, you will have taken a share of it, and if what you follow is more correct than what we follow, we will have taken a share of it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ to the end of the surah."

وأخْرَجَ عَبْدُ بْنُ حُمَيْدٍ، وابْنُ المُنْذِرِ، وابْنُ مَرْدَوَيْهِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّ قُرَيْشًا قالَتْ: لَوِ اسْتَلَمْتَ آلِهَتَنا لَعَبَدْنا إلَهَكَ، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ السُّورَةَ كُلَّها.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that Quraysh said: "If you touched our gods, we would worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾, the whole surah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 109, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Ikrimah.

It is Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and to Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The surah ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ was revealed in Medina."

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Jabir, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this surah and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in the two rak'ahs of the tawaf."

Also in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib some twenty times, or about ten times: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

al-Hakim narrated and graded as sahih from Ubayy, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would perform the witr with ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Muhammad ibn Nasr and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ equals one third of the Qur'an, and ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ equals one quarter of the Qur'an, and he used to recite both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ it is for him equal to a quarter of the Qur'an.'"

al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ it is as if he recited a quarter of the Qur'an, and whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ it is as if he recited a third of the Qur'an."

Ahmad, Ibn al-Durays, al-Baghawi, and Humayd ibn Zanjawayh in his Targhib narrated from a shaykh who met the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and he passed by a man reciting ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, and he said: 'As for this one, he has been freed from shirk.' Then another was reciting ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By it, Paradise has become obligatory for him.'" In another narration: "As for this one, he has been forgiven."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from his father, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, teach me what I should say when I go to my bed. He said: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, then sleep upon its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i, from his father, as a marfu' report, the same as it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah al-Ashja'i: 'When you come to your resting place for sleep, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, for when you say it, you have become free from shirk.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from al-Harith ibn Jabalah, and al-Tabarani said from Jabalah ibn Harithah, who is the brother of Zayd ibn Harithah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, teach me something to say when I sleep. He said: 'When you take your resting place at night, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until you reach its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Mu'adh: 'Recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"

Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not direct you to a word that will save you from associating partners with Allah: that you recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ when you sleep."

al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khabbab that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you take your resting place, recite ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) never came to his bed except that he recited ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ until he finished."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever meets Allah with two surahs, there is no reckoning for him: ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il and Ibn al-Durays narrated from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in a night, he has done much and done well."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The alif and lam in ﴿O you who disbelieve﴾ are for the category (li-l-jins). However, since the verse is addressed to those whom Allah knew in His knowledge would die upon their disbelief (p-1662), the intended meaning of this generality is the specific group of those who were like that; for among the disbelievers at the time of the revelation of this verse were those who embraced Islam and worshipped Allah, glorified be He.

The occasion of revelation of this surah is that the disbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to worship their gods for a year, and they would worship his God for a year.

So Allah, glorified be He, commanded him to say to them: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning: I will not do what you demand of me, namely worshipping what you worship of idols. It was said that the intended meaning concerns the future time, because the negating particle lā (not) generally does not enter except upon the present-future imperfect verb, just as mā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the present.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor will you do in the future what I demand from you of worshipping my God.

﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: nor have I ever, in what has passed, been a worshipper of what you have worshipped, and the sense is: this has not been known of me.

﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning: nor have you worshipped at any time what I am upon worshipping. So it was said, and this is according to the opinion of the one who said there is no repetition in these verses, because the first clause is for negating worship in the future, for the reason we previously mentioned that lā does not enter except upon an imperfect verb with the meaning of the future. The evidence for this is that lan is an emphasis of what lā negates.

al-Khalil said regarding "lan": its origin is lā, so the meaning is: I will not worship what you worship in the future, nor will you be worshippers in the future of what I seek of worship of my God.

Then he said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: and I am not, at present, a worshipper of your worshipped, nor are you, at present, worshippers of my worshipped.

It was also said the opposite of this, namely that the first two clauses are for the present, and the last two clauses are for the future, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as if someone said: "I am striking Zayd, and I am killing 'Amr," for it is not understood from it except the future.

al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: I will not worship, from now on, what you worship; nor will you be worshippers, from now on, of what I worship; nor am I, in the future, a worshipper of what you have worshipped; nor will you, in the future, be worshippers of what I worship.

al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) negated by this surah his worshipping of their gods for himself, both at present and in the future, and he negated for them the worship of Allah, both at present and in the future.

It was said that each of them is suitable for both the present and the future, but we specify one of them for the present and the second for the future, to avoid repetition.

All of this contains from artificiality and forcing what is not hidden from an impartial person. As for making His saying "nor will I worship what you worship" refer to the future, although it is correct according to the requirement of the Arabic language, it does not work to make His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ refer to the future; because the clause is nominal, and it indicates permanence and constancy at all times, so the entry of negation upon it removes what it indicates of permanence and constancy at all times. And if its being taken as the future were correct, the same would apply to His saying ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ and to His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, so the saying that the two latter clauses refer to the present does not hold. And just as this is refuted, the opposite of what was said is refuted too; because the second, third, and fourth clauses are all nominal clauses introduced by pronouns, which are the subject in each of them, reporting about it with the active participle that governs what follows it, all negated by a single particle, namely the word lā in each of them. So how can it be valid, with this unity, to claim that their meanings in the present and the future are different?

As for the statement of the one who said that each of them is suitable for the present and the future, it is an admission by him of repetition; for taking this in one sense and that in another sense while the wording is one is a matter of arbitrary decision for which no evidence points.

Once this is established for you, know that the Qur'an was revealed in the tongue of the Arabs, and among their practices which cannot be denied and their usages which cannot be rejected is that when they want emphasis they repeat, just as among their practices is that when they want brevity they be concise. This is known to everyone who has knowledge of the Arabic language, and this does not need proof, for proof is sought only for what is obscure, and is demonstrated only for what is disputed.

As for what is so clear, evident, and manifest that no doubter doubts it and no skeptic is uncertain about it, it needs no lengthening and no multiplying of talk and debate.

Among this there occurs in the Qur'an what every reciter of the Qur'an knows, and it perhaps abounds in some surahs, as in Surah al-Rahman and Surah al-Mursalat. In the poetry of the Arabs there is from this what cannot be enumerated, and among it is the saying of the poet:

"O Bakr, rally for me Kulayb; O Bakr, where, where is the flight?"

And another's saying:

"Would that you had asked the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, where, where is ours?"

And another's saying:

"O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, O 'Alqamah, the best of Tamim, all of it, and its most noble."

And another's saying:

"Ah, O you, be safe, then be safe, then be safe, three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And another's saying:

"O Ja'far, O Ja'far, O Ja'far, if I am short, you are shorter."

And another's saying:

"Your pursuers have come to you, your pursuers have come to you; hold back, hold back."

It is established from the Truthful and Truly Believed One (ﷺ), and he was the most eloquent of those who spoke the tongue of the Arabs, that when he spoke a word he would repeat it three times. When you know this, the benefit of the emphasis that occurs in the surah is to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would answer them in what they asked of him, namely worshipping their gods. Allah, glorified be He, expressed with "mā," which is used for non-rational beings, in the four positions, because that is permissible, as in His saying: "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" and similar; and the point of this is that the speech proceeds in one pattern and does not vary.

It was said that He intended the attribute, as if He said: I do not worship falsehood, and you do not worship truth.

It was said that "mā" in the four positions is the verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) and not the relative: that is, "I do not worship your worship, and you are not worshippers of my worship," etc.

The clause ﴿For you is your religion﴾ is a resumptive clause establishing His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ and His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, just as His saying ﴿and for me is my religion﴾ establishes His saying ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ in both places (p-1663): that is, if you are content with your religion, then I am content with my religion, as in His saying ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 139]. The meaning is: your religion, which is polytheism, is restricted to being attained by you and does not pass beyond you to being attained by me, as you hope; and my religion, which is monotheism, is restricted to being attained by me and does not pass beyond me to being attained by you.

It was said the meaning is: for you is your recompense, and for me is my recompense; because religion means recompense.

It was said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and it was said it is not abrogated, because they are statements, and statements are not subject to abrogation.

Al-Jumhur read the yā' in His saying "wa-liya" with sukun; Nafi', Hisham, Hafs, and al-Bazzi read it with fatah.

Al-Jumhur also read with the deletion of the yā' in "dini," both in pause and in continuation; Nasr ibn 'Asim, Salam, and Ya'qub retained it both in continuation and in pause.

They said: because it is a noun, it is not deleted.

It is answered that its deletion for the sake of the rhyme-endings (fawasil) is permissible even though it is a noun.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 109, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 2):

وقَدْ أخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، والطَّبَرانِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ «أنَّ قُرَيْشًا دَعَتْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ إلى أنْ يُعْطُوهُ مالًا فَيَكُونُ أغْنى رَجُلٍ بِمَكَّةَ ويُزَوِّجُوهُ ما أرادَ مِنَ النِّساءِ، فَقالُوا: هَذا لَكَ يا مُحَمَّدُ وكُفَّ عَنْ شَتْمِ آلِهَتِنا ولا تَذْكُرْها بِسُوءٍ، فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ فَإنّا نَعْرِضُ عَلَيْكَ خَصْلَةً واحِدَةً ولَكَ فِيها صَلاحٌ، قالَ: ما هي ؟ قالُوا: تَعْبُدُ آلِهَتَنا سَنَةً ونَعْبُدُ إلَهَكَ سَنَةً، قالَ: حَتّى أنْظُرَ ما يَأْتِينِي مِن رَبِّي، فَجاءَ الوَحْيُ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ ﴿لا أعْبُدُ ما تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ، وأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ أفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ تَأْمُرُونِّي أعْبُدُ أيُّها الجاهِلُونَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٤] إلى قَوْلِهِ: ﴿بَلِ اللَّهَ فاعْبُدْ وكُنْ مِنَ الشّاكِرِينَ﴾ [الزمر: ٦٦]» .

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to accept wealth from them, so that he would become the richest man in Makkah, and that they would marry him to whichever women he wished. They said: 'This is for you, O Muhammad, but cease reviling our gods and do not speak ill of them. If you do not do so, we offer you one proposal, and in it there is benefit for you.' He said: 'What is it?' They said: 'You worship our gods for one year, and we will worship your God for one year.' He said: 'Wait until I see what comes to me from my Lord.' Then revelation came from Allah: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ to the end of the surah. And Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64] to His words: ﴿Rather, worship Allah and be among the thankful﴾ [al-Zumar: 66]."

وأخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ، وابْنُ أبِي حاتِمٍ، وابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ في المَصاحِفِ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ مِينا مَوْلى أبِي البُحْتُرِيِّ قالَ لَقِيَ الوَلِيدُ بْنُ المُغِيرَةِ، والعاصُ بْنُ وائِلٍ، والأسْوَدُ بْنُ المُطَّلِبِ، وأُمَيَّةُ بْنُ خَلَفٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ قالُوا: يا مُحَمَّدُ هَلُمَّ فَلْنَعْبُدْ ما تَعْبُدُ وتَعْبُدْ ما نَعْبُدُ، ونَشْتَرِكْ نَحْنُ وأنْتَ في أمْرِنا كُلِّهِ، فَإنْ كانَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ كُنْتَ قَدْ أخَذْتَ مِنهُ حَظًّا، وإنْ كانَ الَّذِي أنْتَ عَلَيْهِ أصَحَّ مِنَ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ كُنّا قَدْ أخَذْنا مِنهُ حَظًّا، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ إلى آخِرِ السُّورَةِ.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in (his book) al-Masahif (the codices of the Qur'an) narrated from Sa'id ibn Mina, the mawla (freedman) of Abu al-Bukhturi, who said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, come, let us worship what you worship and you worship what we worship, and let us share with you in all of our affair. If what we follow is more correct than what you follow, you will have taken a share of it, and if what you follow is more correct than what we follow, we will have taken a share of it.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾ to the end of the surah."

وأخْرَجَ عَبْدُ بْنُ حُمَيْدٍ، وابْنُ المُنْذِرِ، وابْنُ مَرْدَوَيْهِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّ قُرَيْشًا قالَتْ: لَوِ اسْتَلَمْتَ آلِهَتَنا لَعَبَدْنا إلَهَكَ، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ ﴿قُلْ ياأيُّها الكافِرُونَ﴾ السُّورَةَ كُلَّها.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that Quraysh said: "If you touched our gods, we would worship your God." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers!"﴾, the whole surah.
